tob-4032: François Rabelais’s roaring epic follows two giants — Gargantua and his son Pantagruel — through a France of monks, scholars, and wars, in prose stuffed with jokes, lists, and earthy humor. Under the laughter runs a scholar’s plea for learning and free minds. It is the great comic crown of the French Renaissance.
tob-4166-2832: Andrew Lang’s Myth, Ritual and Religion holds that the wild, savage bits in Greek tale are leftovers of an older mind — not late rot. This first volume pleads his case with wit and a flood of witnesses. The book took on the reigning myth-theories of the day.
tob-4214-10732: Studies in Pessimism binds Schopenhauer’s blackest and most famed pages — on the emptiness of being, on self-murder, on why bliss is a cheat. Brief, quotable, and crushing. Saunders’s renderings made the Will’s philosopher an English cult-figure.
tob-0132: The Hatha Yoga Pradipika is the classic handbook of body-yoga — postures, breath-work, and the waking of the coiled power. Set down in the 1400s by Svatmarama, it ordered the yogic body arts into a system. The text is the groundwork of all latter-day hatha yoga.
tob-4132: Mead’s fourth Echoes booklet gives the Hymn of Jesus — the round-dance song from the Acts of John, where Christ leads his followers in a mystic ring-dance. His notes unfold the song’s Gnostic sense. The booklet made a little-known treasure readable for all.
tob-10032: Mackail’s Englishing of Virgil’s Herd-Songs gives the ten shepherd poems — herdsmen singing love and loss in a golden countryside. The songs founded herd-poetry as a western kind. The fourth song’s wonder-child made Virgil Christendom’s seer. This printing bears his music to our readers.
tob-13532: Johann Weyer’s Fiend-Tricks — 1563 — is the landmark doubting work on witch-hunting. The Dutch leech held blamed witches black-biled souls, not devil’s servants. His kindly tract withstood the witch-hunters of his day. The book is a milestone in soul-leech story.
cia-0000112332: A March 1990 report on the Soviet Union establishing a state center for the study of UFOs. Glasnost had opened the skies to public curiosity, and the state decided to organize it. The CIA clipped the announcement with the same care it gave missile tests — because you never knew what the other side's strange programs really were.
cia-0000112832: An October 1945 file on Juan Tria, marked for espionage. The war was over, but the accounting of spies went on — every network had to be mapped before its members disappeared. The entry is one name in the great postwar sorting of who had served whom.
cia-0000119732: An Eastern Europe roundup from September 1956 focused on the Hungarian situation. Regional surveys put Hungary's unrest in context — Poland was stirring too, and Moscow was watching both. The document shows analysts connecting the tremors across the Soviet bloc.
cia-0000120632: A memorandum of an August 1962 meeting with the president about Cuba — two months before the missile crisis. Kennedy and his advisors were already deep in the Cuba problem. The document is a glimpse into the White House on the eve of the Cold War's most dangerous fortnight.
cia-0000124332: A January 1960 document, its title carrying the archive's typo, with information on American POWs who were not repatriated. Years after the armistice, some prisoners never came home — and the questions never closed. The entry confronts the war's most painful loose end.
cia-0000126932: An untitled 1983 list of names and memberships — the estimated date is all the catalog offers. Membership lists were the wiring diagrams of organizations: who belonged, and to what. The entry is a roster awaiting its context — the full text may supply it.
cia-0000132232: Situation Report 549 on the status of the oil spill and political developments. The deliberate spill was becoming one of the war's defining images — beaches blackened, wildlife dying. The document tracks the environmental front alongside the diplomatic one.
cia-0000132432: A January 1960 report on Cuban arms purchases. A revolution expecting invasion shops for guns — and Havana was shopping in the East. The document follows the weapons: the island, arming.
cia-0000132632: A June 1960 roundup titled Developments in Cuba. The revolution's second year was bringing radicalization — the moderates gone, the communists rising. The document is the trend, noted: the island, hardening.
cia-0000135832: An estimated 1954 study of assassination — the CIA's infamous how-to manual for killing foreign leaders. Declassified, it remains shocking: murder, methodized. The document is the manual: the craft, codified — the agency's darkest text.
cia-0000135932: A 1954 cable from LINCOLN requesting follow-up on a public reply to a white paper. The propaganda war had its paperwork. The document is the follow-up: the reply, chased.
cia-0000136232: The daily operations situation report number three, 1954. The invasion's daily pulse. The document is the count: the third day, reported.
cia-0000136932: A 1954 cable to the senior representative at LINCOLN on ODYOKE sending loads of arms — the truncated title cuts off to whom. The weapons pipeline. The document is the shipment: the arms, sent.
cia-0000137332: An estimated 1960 memorandum for the record transmitting the attached papers — the archive's spelling says fotr and atached, the truncated title cuts off the subject. The cover memo. The entry is the transmittal: the papers, forwarded — through typos.
un-ga-res-32: United Nations General Assembly Resolution 32, adopted in 1946 — among the very first resolutions of the newborn United Nations. The catalog record preserves its number and date; the full text carries its subject. The resolution is the artifact: the young UN, deciding.
un-ga-res-a-69-32: General Assembly Resolution A/69/32, adopted in 2014 — session and year agree. A decision of the modern Assembly. The designation is certain; the subject belongs to the text.
un-sc-res-32: Security Council Resolution 32, adopted in 1947. The early Council's work. The designation and year are preserved; the act is in the text.
un-sc-res-232: Security Council Resolution 232, cataloged with the year 1960 — though the famous sanctions resolution of that number belongs to 1966, a mismatch. The designation is kept; the date is doubted — and the subject is left to the text.
un-sc-res-1332: Security Council Resolution 1332, adopted in 2000 — aligned. The millennium Council at work. The number and year survive; the decision lives in the text.
un-sc-res-1532: Security Council Resolution 1532, adopted in 2004 — aligned. The Council's business continued. The number and year survive; the decision lives in the text.
un-sc-res-1632: Security Council Resolution 1632, adopted in 2005 — aligned. The Council deciding. The number and year are preserved; the decision belongs to the text.
un-sc-res-1732: Security Council Resolution 1732, adopted in 2006 — aligned. The deliberations continued. The number and year survive; the decision lives in the text.
un-sc-res-1932: Security Council Resolution 1932, cataloged with the year 2011 — the numbering suggests 2010, a small inconsistency. The designation is kept; the date is questioned.
cia-0000135732: An estimated 1961 CIA file of Spanish-text 2506 Brigade documents — number 0000135732, the archive's date approximate. The roughly dated documents. The entry is the roughness: the dating, soft.
cia-0000136632: A 1961 CIA file of Spanish-text 2506 Brigade documents, numbered 0000136632 — closing this batch. The Bay of Pigs papers, preserved. The entry is the close: the batch, complete.
plos-pone-0000032: A 2006 PLOS ONE paper: a mouse stromal response to tumor invasion predicts prostate and breast cancer outcomes — the truncated title suggests. The tissue around the tumor tells the prognosis. The paper is the prediction: the stroma, prophetic.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d32: The ambassador in Egypt, Kirk, to the Secretary of State — the truncated title cuts off the date — Document 32. Cairo's embassy reported. The cable is the embassy's: the ambassador, informing.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d132: The president's secretary Early to the secretaries of State, War — the truncated title cuts off the rest — Document 132. The White House staff's paper. The memo is the staffwork: Early, writing.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d232: A memorandum by the United States Chiefs of Staff, November 18, 1943 — Document 232. A sixth that day. The memo is the sixth: the staff, tireless.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d332: The President to the minister in Egypt, Kirk — the truncated title cuts off the date — Document 332. The White House wrote Cairo's legation. The message is the legation: Kirk, instructed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d432: The president's special assistant Hopkins to the ambassador in Turkey — the truncated title cuts off the rest — Document 432. The insider wrote Ankara's envoy. The cable is the insider's: Hopkins, to Steinhardt.
arxiv-2605-08832: Filling in missing pieces of a fluid simulation — inpainting — is usually done with expensive physics solvers. This 2026 paper takes a self-supervised learning approach instead, training a model to reconstruct fluid behavior from surrounding context without labeled examples. The work points toward cheaper, context-driven fluid simulation.
arxiv-2605-08932: Haloscopes hunt axions — hypothetical dark-matter particles — by coaxing them to convert into light inside tuned cavities. J.M. García-Barceló, Jose R. Navarro-Madrid, and colleagues study a multicavity design built as hexagonal coaxial haloscopes. The 2026 paper is dark-matter instrumentation.
arxiv-2605-09232: Smart-home gadgets learning together must not leak their owners' lives. John Cartmell and Alexander Williams build a unified threat model and evaluation framework for privacy-preserving distributed learning in IoT systems. The 2026 paper is security methodology for the Internet of Things.
arxiv-2605-09432: IP over avian carriers — the famous RFC 1149 joke — gets a serious algorithmic treatment. Matthias Bentert, Shay Kutten, Darya Melnyk, and colleagues analyze the carrier pigeon internet protocol with a lighthearted but rigorous eye. The 2026 paper is networking theory that does not take itself too seriously.
arxiv-2605-09732: Width-based dynamic programming solves hard problems by bounding their complexity; TreeWidzard automates the method — and proves theorems along the way. Mateus de Oliveira Oliveira and Sam Urmian build the engine. The 2026 paper is automated reasoning with real mathematical guarantees.
arxiv-2605-09832: Proteins wiggle through conformational ensembles, and Boltz-2 predicts structures — but test-time supervision with cryo-EM density maps sharpens the picture. Jay Shenoy, Miro Astore, Axel Levy, and colleagues model atomic ensembles that way. The 2026 paper is structural biology with test-time learning.
arxiv-2605-10032: Plant marker reasoning — identifying genetic markers from evidence — across multiple species: PlantMarkerBench. Sajib Acharjee Dip, Song Li, and colleagues build the multi-species benchmark for evidence-grounded reasoning. The 2026 paper is plant genomics AI with receipts. It grounds plant reasoning in evidence.
plos-pone-0003432: Entomologists checked whether a mosquito-killing microbe overstays its welcome in this 2008 field study. Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis, or Bti, is a biological alternative to chemical insecticides, but the team found it persists in mosquito habitats far longer than expected. That staying power matters for both effectiveness and for watching unintended ecological effects.
plos-pone-0003532: Biogeographers reconstructed how common voles colonized Europe in this 2008 paper. Combining DNA evidence with fossils, they traced the rodents' spread through the ice ages' climatic swings. The colonization story shows how Quaternary cycles repeatedly redrew the map of biodiversity, with lessons for how species may move as climates shift again.
plos-pone-0003632: Cancer biologists Seoane, Iglesias, and Gonzalez found a lost guardian speeding tumors in this 2008 paper. When the retinoblastoma protein is gone, cells' response to DNA damage changes in ways that favor tumor progression, partly by undermining the senescence barrier. The work shows how losing one brake rewires the whole safety system.
plos-pone-0003732: In 2008, Huffard, Caldwell, and DeLoach gave wild octopuses photo IDs. Each Wunderpus photogenicus octopus wears a one-of-a-kind body color pattern, letting researchers tell individuals apart from photographs alone. The non-invasive tracking opens long-term studies of these shy, short-lived animals in the wild.
plos-pone-0003832: Petkova and Ehrsson gave volunteers an out-of-body swap in this 2008 paper. Using a perceptual illusion, participants felt they inhabited another person's body. The body-swap experiment probes how the brain decides which body is mine, a question at the root of selfhood.
plos-pone-0003932: In 2008, Kidder, Yang, and Palmer mapped where two stem-cell masters sit on DNA. Across the genome, they charted the promoter spots occupied by Stat3 and c-Myc. Both factors proved essential for keeping embryonic stem cells unspecialized. The occupancy map shows the control circuitry of pluripotency itself.
plos-pone-0004032: In 2008, Agrawal and Banerjee gave a gene-silencing protein a second job. Human Polycomb 2 proved to be a SUMO E3 ligase, tagging proteins for modification. The ligase activity eased substrate inhibition of the cystathionine beta-synthase enzyme. The surprising double duty links epigenetic control to sulfur amino-acid metabolism.
plos-pone-0004132: In 2009, Kucera, Strilic, and Regener rebuilt the first blood vessels in theory. They showed ancestral vascular tubes forming through basal cell surfaces. No endothelial cells needed: the primitive lumen arose from cell bases. The model rewinds vessel evolution to its roots.
plos-pone-0004232: In 2009, Mellata, Touchman, and Curtiss decoded a poultry-killer plasmid. The full sequence of plasmid pAPEC-1 from avian pathogenic E. coli was fully mapped. Comparative analysis revealed its virulence cargo clearly. The new blueprint aids vaccines against deadly bird E. coli.
plos-pone-0004332: In 2009, Morse, Peterson, and Islam-Faridi sized up pine genomes. Genome size and complexity evolution in pines was traced. The giant gymnosperm genomes grew through repeat expansion. The study maps conifer genome history. The work explains how pines became genomic giants.
plos-pone-0358332: Quiz champions seem to read a question and instantly know where the answer hides. This study investigated which words trivia experts focus on, then compared human strategies with an AI judge’s — the ‘LLM-as-a-judge’ approach. The human-AI comparison reveals what expert intuition catches that algorithms notice differently, and vice versa.
plos-pone-0356632: Metacognitive training helps people with psychosis question their own distorted thinking — but do men and women improve differently? Drawing on a large harmonized database, this paper traced sex-specific symptom trajectories after the training. The diverging paths suggest therapy for psychosis may need to be tuned by sex.
plos-pone-0357232: This paper put montmorillonite-impregnated burnt-red clay through full microstructural and physicochemical characterization, with statistical evaluation of strength and durability. The results quantify what the clay treatment adds to mechanical performance — and whether it holds up under weathering.
plos-pone-0358232: Potato cyst nematodes devastate crops — and their HYP1 gene varies in ways scientists couldn’t explain. This paper showed diversity at the HYP1 locus does not result from developmentally programmed somatic mutations. Ruling out that mechanism narrows the hunt considerably for where the variation really comes from.
plos-pone-0355932: Who gets to decide in rural Ethiopian households — on crops, on spending, on daily life? This paper modeled the determinants of women’s decision-making autonomy on agriculture and household matters using a mixed-effects beta regression tree. The analysis reveals which factors genuinely empower women to decide.
plos-pone-0357032: Vision loss is rising across the Gulf states — and planners need to see it coming. This analysis tracked visual impairment trends in the Gulf Council Countries from 1990 to 2021, with time-series predictions to 2030. The forecasts give eye-care systems a decade of warning to prepare.
plos-pone-0357832: Some patients end up living in hospitals for months — with nowhere else to go. This paper studied long-term hospital stays at a tertiary infectious disease hospital in Manaus, deep in the Brazilian Amazon, where the hospital becomes the only place to live. The accounts expose a hidden crisis of abandonment and care.
plos-pone-0339732: River dunes behave strangely where sand gives way to gravel. This paper studied the decoupled morphodynamic responses of dune crests and localized scour across the sand-gravel transition in straight alluvial channels. The findings improve the models engineers use to predict river behavior.
plos-pone-0352132: Racialized mothers in Canada face distinct postpartum mental health challenges that research has largely ignored. This scoping review protocol will systematically map the evidence on their experiences. The planned review centers mothers whom the literature has marginalized.
plos-pone-0344932: Preserving whole brains — even aldehyde-fixed ones — pushes cryobiology to its limits. This paper explored the cryopreservation of aldehyde-fixed whole brains. The techniques inch toward a future where entire brains might be banked for research — or for far more ambitious purposes.
plos-pone-0355232: Teaching wears on the body as well as the mind. This paper studied the psychophysiological correlates of professional experience among female secondary school teachers in Kazakhstan. The findings reveal how years in the classroom etch themselves into teachers’ stress physiology — and what might protect them.
plos-pone-0355332: Bio-electrochemical reactors can strip organic carbon from wastewater — especially with nanoparticle help. This paper studied multi-phase reactions for organic carbon removal using Fe2O3-synthesized nanoparticles. The nanoparticle-enhanced process points toward cheaper, greener wastewater treatment.
plos-pone-0351932: Premature babies on intravenous nutrition need precisely verified doses — errors can be fatal. This paper developed and validated an intelligent weight verification management system for neonatal ready-to-use parenteral nutrition infusions. The automated verification adds a safety net where tiny patients can least afford mistakes.
plos-pone-0353932: Young people with chronic conditions often fall off a cliff when aging out of pediatric care. The COCCOS study protocol outlines a multicentric quasi-experimental study of a healthcare transition program for these youths. The planned research tests whether structured transition support keeps vulnerable young adults in care.
plos-pone-0355832: Losing smell and taste was COVID-19’s strangest signature — and genes may explain who suffered it. This genome-wide machine learning analysis probed anosmia and ageusia in COVID-19 patients. The ML-driven genetics point to the biological pathways that stole millions of people’s senses of smell and taste.
plos-pone-0345032: Tirzepatide — the blockbuster diabetes and weight-loss drug — is judged by a triple endpoint. This paper examined achieving body weight reduction thresholds plus systolic blood pressure drops of at least 5 mmHg and non-HDL cholesterol under 130 mg/dL with the drug. The composite analysis shows how many patients hit the full trifecta of metabolic benefit.
plos-pone-0335832: CDO1 gene methylation might distinguish gastric cancer from mere chronic gastritis. This comparative study examined CDO1 promoter methylation in gastric cancer versus H. pylori-associated gastritis, assessing diagnostic performance. The epigenetic marker could spare patients unnecessary invasive workups — or catch cancers earlier.
plos-pone-0353232: Academics timing parenthood around tenure face a cruel calculus. This paper examined the relationship between tenure and fertility among academics — asking when the ‘best time’ to become a parent really is. The findings expose how academic career structures penalize reproduction — and who pays the price.
plos-pone-0343832: Tourists want drone photography — and cultural sites want it managed smartly. This paper designed and implemented a microservice-based self-service drone aerial photography system for smart cultural tourism. The system lets visitors capture stunning aerial views without endangering heritage — or each other.
plos-pone-0355732: Cancer patients in acute care need navigation — and physiotherapists might guide them. This Ontario-wide modified Delphi study proposed using a physiotherapist navigator in acute cancer care. The expert consensus maps a new role that could keep cancer patients moving — literally and figuratively — through treatment.
europmc-pmc2797632: Bacteria that grow fast leave a signature in their genomes, and this 2010 paper explores how to read it. The authors show that growth-related patterns in DNA can reveal how microbes behave in environmental samples, without growing them in the lab. The approach brings new power to metagenomics, the study of microbial communities from DNA alone.
europmc-pmc2810332: Malaria rapid tests usually hunt for two parasite proteins, pfhrp2 and pfhrp3, but some parasites in the Peruvian Amazon have lost both genes. This 2010 paper reports that a large share of local P. falciparum isolates lack them. The finding warns that standard tests may miss infections there. It pushed health programs to rethink diagnostic strategy in the region.
europmc-pmc2864732: As climates shift, species must adapt, bend, or die. This 2010 paper works toward a predictive theory of adaptation, plasticity, and extinction in a changing world. The authors fuse models into one framework. Their synthesis aids forecasts of who survives rapid change.
europmc-pmc2882432: Babies born even slightly early may face learning hurdles. This 2010 study of 407,503 schoolchildren links gestational age at delivery to special educational need. The authors' huge cohort reveals a gradient of risk. Their finding argues for weighing every week of pregnancy.
europmc-pmc2896632: KRAS is among the most mutated genes in cancer, yet long undruggable. This 2010 review covers the clinical relevance of KRAS in human cancers. The authors weigh its role as marker and target. Their overview captured the state of play before KRAS drugs finally arrived.
europmc-pmc2902432: Niemann-Pick disease type C traps cholesterol inside cells, slowly wrecking organs. This 2010 review covers the rare inherited disorder, its course, and its care. The author distills hard-won knowledge for a cruel diagnosis. Their review guides families and doctors facing it.
europmc-pmc2910032: Immune cells shift with age, and this 2010 paper tracks the drift. The authors map age-dependent changes in monocyte subsets and related chemokine pathways in healthy adults. Their profiles show immunity remodeling over decades. The data became a baseline for aging research.
europmc-pmc2936532: Plants starved of phosphorus flip a master switch to cope. This 2010 paper shows one central control system runs most gene on-off responses to phosphate hunger in Arabidopsis. The authors map the command center. Their work aids breeding crops for poor soils.
europmc-pmc2950132: Lung-germ shots must match the strains going around to shield kids. This 2010 paper sizes up which germ types cause grave lung disease in young children worldwide. The authors' world survey steers shot design. Their data shaped jab programs. New combo shots leaned on its type maps.
europmc-pmc2982832: Ancient mitochondrial DNA can be fished out in bulk. This 2010 paper shows how to capture many mitochondrial genomes at once from PCR bits. The authors' method speeds old-DNA work. Their trick aided Pääbo's Neanderthal research. Bone dust yields whole genomes with the trick.
europmc-pmc3019132: Low blood protein predicts cancer death. This 2010 review finds low albumin before treatment forecasts worse cancer survival. The authors' pooling confirms the marker. Their work aids prognosis. A cheap blood test carries the signal. Malnourished patients fare worst of all.
europmc-pmc6510332: Premature babies in intensive care are wired up with stiff sensors that glue painfully to their fragile skin. This paper presents a gentler answer: two soft, skin-thin wireless patches that work as a pair. They track vital signs and do the number-crunching right on the sensor, freeing tiny patients from cables and harsh adhesives.
europmc-pmc6518732: Triple-negative breast cancer lacks the three receptors that most breast-cancer drugs target, leaving few treatment options. This systematic review evaluates STAT3 - a signaling protein that helps these tumors grow and resist therapy - as a drug target. The authors sift the evidence for medicines that block STAT3, outlining a path toward badly needed new treatments.
europmc-pmc6530332: Cancer cells decorate their proteins with abnormal sugar chains - a process called glycosylation - and those sugary coatings reshape the tumor's surroundings. This review shows how altered glycans drive cancer's hallmark behaviors: growth, invasion, and immune evasion. Because the sugar patterns are distinctive, they also offer targets for new diagnostics and therapies.
europmc-pmc6540032: Skin aging starts deep: in the dermis, collagen fibers fragment, clump, and dwindle, while the fibroblasts that maintain them falter. This review maps the molecular machinery of dermal aging - the enzymes, signals, and structural failures involved. It also surveys anti-aging approaches, from retinoids to emerging therapies, judging each against the underlying biology.
europmc-pmc6547132: Brain scans can now spot Alzheimer's two hallmark lesions - amyloid plaques and tau tangles - in living people. Tracking healthy older adults over years, researchers watched both proteins pile up and linked their buildup to slipping memory and thinking. The longitudinal study pins down how amyloid and tau team up to erode cognition before symptoms appear.
europmc-pmc6565732: Two hours a week in parks or woods marks a threshold: people hitting at least 120 minutes of nature contact reported notably better health and wellbeing. The large UK study found the benefit held across ages and backgrounds, then tapered off. The finding gives doctors and planners a concrete, achievable nature prescription.
europmc-pmc6646332: Gut microbes make acetate - and this humble molecule helps lungs fight RSV. In mice, microbiota-derived acetate engaged the GPR43 receptor and interferon defenses to blunt respiratory syncytial virus. The gut-lung axis emerges as a real defense line, with diet-tweakable implications.
europmc-pmc6658332: Monocytes were once seen as a uniform battalion - now they are a diverse cast with distinct cancer roles. This review maps monocyte heterogeneity: the subtypes, what each does in tumors, and how they shape progression. Understanding the cast helps target the troublemakers while sparing the helpers.
europmc-pmc6658832: Farmers already deploy helpful microbes against crop diseases - but how do these biocontrol agents actually work? This review goes beyond 'does it work' to how: competition, parasitism, and priming plant defenses. Understanding the modes of action helps deploy microbial allies more wisely.
europmc-pmc6677832: Colorectal tumors get a boost from a long non-coding RNA called GLCC1, which steadies the c-Myc cancer protein and revs up sugar metabolism. This study untangles the chain in bowel cancer. Knocking down GLCC1 could brake both growth and the tumor's sweet tooth.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-32: GAO warned Congress in 2007 that the money world was outgrowing its minders. Mergers, new money gadgets, and global deals were straining a rulebook built for simpler times. The report, written on the eve of the great crash, reads now like a flare shot up before the fall: the watchers were not set up for the world they had to watch.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-432: NASA's gear was walking off in 2007 — GAO's report says weak controls and thin accountability left space equipment easy to lose or steal. The findings describe a rocket agency with a leaky stockroom and no firm grip on its inventory. The report warns that lost tools can ground missions and burn taxpayer money.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-332: Job rehab lifted earnings but reached few in 2007 — GAO's report says many disability beneficiaries earned more after services, though too few finished. The findings praise the gains and flag the dropouts. The report's push: the program works, so make it reach.
openalex-w7207773232: The film Oppenheimer tells the story of the atomic bomb, and these authors see it as a teaching tool. This article examines how the movie can anchor science lessons on the ties between science, technology, politics, and ethics: who decides what gets built, and who lives with the consequences. It outlines classroom strategies that use the film to spark discussion of real scientific dilemmas. A case for learning science through cinema.
openalex-w7204886632: Laws protecting people with disabilities have been on the books for decades, yet true inclusion is still out of reach. This article looks at the clashing views around special education: the legal promises of inclusion and the social habits that block it. The authors set progress against the contradictions of modern life. Thoughtful rather than preachy, it asks why rights on paper still fail in daily life.
openalex-w7205015932: When police use force, institutional culture shapes the decision as much as the law. This article studies how the culture of the Amazonas military police affects officers' use of graduated force, creating tension between human rights and operational demands. The authors probe where habit overrides restraint. A frank examination of the gap between rights on paper and force on the street.
openalex-w7204464632: Necrotizing enterocolitis is one of the most feared emergencies in newborn care, striking premature and very-low-birth-weight babies. This review gathers what the literature says about its risk factors and warning signs. The authors aim to help neonatologists spot the disease earlier. A clinical review where early recognition can mean the difference for the tiniest patients.
openalex-w4410981132: Japan is pooling its medical images into a giant research resource. This paper introduces J-MID, the Japan Medical Image Database, built on the DICOM standard to power data science. The authors described the big-data platform. A medical-informatics paper of images fueling discovery.
pmc-13466932: A 2026 commentary reviewing the evidence from trials that pit conduction system pacing against traditional cardiac resynchronization therapy. Rather than running a new trial, the authors decode what existing studies actually show about the newer technique. It is a guide for cardiologists weighing whether to adopt it in practice.
pmc-13474932: A 2026 battery paper describing a solid reservoir of potassium superoxide (KO2) that compensates for irreversible capacity loss in sodium–oxygen batteries. Superoxide-based Na–O2 cells are promising but lose charge over cycles, and this reservoir tops it up. The work pushes a next-generation, high-energy battery chemistry closer to practical use.
pmc-13464432: This 2026 cell biology paper describes how stressed cells switch their way of releasing tiny extracellular vesicles — message-carrying bubbles — from a "torn bag" rupture mode to controlled exocytosis. The switch changes how cells broadcast signals under duress. Understanding the mechanism matters because these vesicles influence immunity, cancer, and healing.
pmc-13458932: In this 2026 cardiology paper, researchers examined how PCSK9 inhibitors — powerful cholesterol-lowering drugs — affect circulatory inflammation. Cholesterol and inflammation both drive artery disease, and the study asks whether these drugs calm the blood's inflammatory state too. The answer shapes how the drugs' benefits are understood.
pmc-13431132: A 2026 liver paper showing that neutrophils — front-line immune cells — promote metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease by shipping lipids to liver cells inside extracellular vesicles. The immune system actively feeds the fatty liver, not just inflames it. Blocking the lipid transfer could be a new treatment angle.
pmc-13480432: In this 2026 cardiac surgery paper, hemodynamic measurements from anesthesia induction through cardiopulmonary bypass improved prediction of right ventricular failure after left ventricular assist device implantation. RV failure after LVAD is often fatal, so better prediction is lifesaving. The study adds concrete variables to risk assessment.
pmc-13416232: In this 2026 pilot secondary analysis of a randomized double-blind trial, correcting hyponatremia — low blood sodium — was associated with increased levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), a protein that supports neuron growth. The link between sodium balance and a brain-health marker is unexpected. The pilot suggests a mechanism worth testing.
pmc-13445632: A 2026 evolution paper on the interplay between evolutionary flexibility and diversification in a spider family. Flexibility and diversity don't always go together. The study disentangles their relationship.
pmc-13512732: A 2026 population genetics paper analyzing Yeniseian and Andronovo substrates in the gene pools of indigenous southern Siberian populations via Q and R1a Y-haplogroups. Ancient layers persist in modern genomes. The analysis reconstructs Siberian prehistory.
pmc-13431432: This 2026 surgical oncology paper predicted anastomotic leak after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy and esophagectomy using a dynamic inflammatory and nutritional biomarker model. The dreaded leak needs prediction. The biomarker model is the tool.
pmc-13420532: This 2026 review covered the global epidemiology of MRSA — methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. The superbug's worldwide patterns inform control. The review is the epidemiological reference.
pmc-13422932: This 2026 scoping review asked what is known about fitness, activity, quality of life, and muscle-strengthening in adults with fibromyalgia. Exercise is medicine for fibromyalgia. The review maps the evidence.
pmc-13530832: A 2026 conference poster systematically reviewing mid- to long-term outcomes of MACI cartilage restoration of the knee. The cell-based repair's durability was assessed. The poster synthesizes the evidence.
pmc-13508132: This 2026 paper showed T1R3 — a taste receptor — anchors ACE2 at the lung endothelial surface, attenuating vascular injury after SARS-CoV-2 spike exposure in vitro. The taste-COVID link is surprising. The mechanism is the discovery.
pmc-13506132: A 2026 pediatric trial comparing buffered lidocaine with bicarbonate versus conventional lidocaine for pain management. The buffered sting was less. The trial is the evidence.

arxiv-2606-15932: A survey paper mapping the field of AI that writes and understands code using more than just text — diagrams, screenshots, and other inputs alongside natural language. It goes beyond simple "type a sentence, get code" systems to catalog how models combine many kinds of information. The survey serves as a roadmap for researchers entering this growing area.
arxiv-2606-16032: Milling metal to a precise roughness usually requires trial and error. This paper uses machine learning to work backwards: given the surface finish you want, it designs the milling settings to achieve it. The "roughness-driven inverse design" approach could save manufacturers time and material by getting the parameters right the first time.
arxiv-2606-15832: Training huge machine learning models means solving hard optimization problems with limited memory. SILAGE is a new optimizer that needs little memory, skips full gradient computations, and handles nonconvex problems built from nested sums of functions. The paper presents the algorithm and its theory, aimed at researchers training large-scale models.
arxiv-2606-16232: Life-like 3D scenes built from 'splats' — soft dots of light — look lush yet hog RAM, a snag for small bots that roam. PolyMerge shrinks those splats inside tight gem wraps that still vouch safe paths. Bots get slim maps with safe-roam proof baked in.
arxiv-2606-16332: Running large language models fast means squeezing every drop from the hardware. SME (Scalable Matrix Extensions) are new CPU instructions for matrix math, and SMEPilot characterizes and optimizes LLM inference on them. The paper gives systems engineers measurements and techniques for speeding up AI serving on SME-capable processors.
arxiv-2606-16632: Atom ear-horns gauge pull and spin with hair care — yet hue-shift (Doppler) smears the tone. This paper stills the smear with quirk lifts and poise-state ruses in a split-beam ear-horn. For atom pros who'd field true quirk gauges. Still tones, true reads.
